## Risks and Mitigations

| # | Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Firehose cutover drops in-flight records | Low | Medium | Old bucket retained during migration; any stragglers copied by a second `--verify-only` pass; documented in the runbook. |
| 2 | CANDIDATE records in model registry reference the deleted bucket | Medium | High | Add explicit task to update all CANDIDATE records' `s3_bucket` field before deleting the old bucket. Block old-bucket deletion on this step. |
| 3 | Downstream code still has a hardcoded `ccet-ml-models-{env}` after the refactor | Medium | Medium | Grep-based CI check (new lint rule): no occurrences of `ccet-ml-datasets-` or `ccet-ml-models-` or `ccet-benchmark-reports-` as string literals outside this spec's doc files. |
| 4 | CDK snapshot tests break widely after the refactor | High | Low | Expected — regenerate snapshots atomically in the same PR. Task list reflects this. |
| 5 | Operator forgets to run `migrate_s3_storage.py` between stacks 1 and 2 | Low | High | `cdk/deploy.py` gains an explicit pre-flight check: if `/ccet/{env}/storage/migration-complete` sentinel SSM parameter is missing, is not valid JSON, or is missing a `completed_at` field, fail downstream deploys with a clear error instructing the operator to run migration (per Prompt 5 A1 canonical JSON shape — Req 18.4). `--skip-migration-check` flag allows re-deploys after migration has been performed. (A3, C5.) |
| 6 | Legacy bucket deletion triggers a Python traceback in some forgotten cron job | Low | Medium | Grep all `scripts/` and `src/` for `ccet-ml-datasets|ccet-ml-models|ccet-benchmark-reports` after refactor — this is an acceptance criterion. |
| 7 | CloudFormation orphans the three old project buckets when their definitions are removed from CDK code | High | Medium | Explicit AWS CLI–based deletion procedure in Task 26 (empty versioned `ccet-ml-datasets-{env}` via `list-object-versions` + `delete-objects`, then `rb`). CloudFormation cannot delete retained-then-removed resources per [AWS DeletionPolicy docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/TemplateReference/aws-attribute-deletionpolicy.html). (C4.) |
| 8 | In-flight SageMaker training/HPO jobs reference old bucket URIs at cutover | Low | Medium | Task 24 adds a pre-flight `aws sagemaker list-training-jobs --status-equals InProgress` check; migration is blocked until no InProgress jobs exist. (B3.) |
| 9 | CANDIDATE model-registry records have `s3_prefix=training-data/...` which maps to `temp/rl-training-exports/...` (not just a bucket rename) | Medium | Medium | Task 20 updated to use the full migration mapping for prefix remapping, not just bucket-name rewriting. (C3.) |

- [ ] 9a. **CI User S3 IAM audit + retarget (NEW per Prompt 5 B2)**
  - **Scope**: `cdk/ci_iam/stack.py`, `cdk/ci_iam/prod_ci_user_stack.py`, `cdk/ci_iam/stage_ci_user_stack.py`.
  - **Evidence (verified via `grepSearch`)**: `cdk/ci_iam/stack.py` line 50 contains `"s3:*"` in `CDK_DEPLOY_ACTIONS`, applied as `Allow` on `Resource=*` (wildcard — all buckets). No old bucket-name literals exist, but the wildcard grant means:
    - (a) the CI user can write to any bucket including `ccet-ml-datasets-{env}` etc., making the Task 29.10 negative test unreliable (a principal with `s3:*` on `*` would succeed in writing to old buckets even after explicit per-bucket IAM revocation on the old buckets);
    - (b) after old buckets are deleted in Task 26, any pipeline step that (incorrectly) addresses an old bucket by name fails with `NoSuchBucket` instead of `AccessDenied`, obscuring misconfigurations.
  - **Bucket import mechanism (NEW per Prompt 6 B1)**: the CI user stack has `STACK_CI_USER: []` (no dependencies) per `cdk/deployment/deployment_ordering.py`, and this Phase 1 preserves that — `STACK_CI_USER` remains first in `DEPLOY_ORDER` and does NOT gain a dependency on `STACK_STORAGE`. To reference the `ccet-{env}` bucket in IAM without creating a CloudFormation dependency, use **string-based import** via `s3.Bucket.from_bucket_name(self, "StorageBucketRef", bucket_name=config.storage_bucket_name)`. IAM `PolicyStatement.Resource` fields may reference ARNs for resources that do not yet exist at CI-user-stack deploy time — the policy is evaluated per-request at runtime by IAM, not at deploy time. This approach (a) keeps `STACK_CI_USER` at the top of `DEPLOY_ORDER` so the CI user exists before any other stack is deployed, and (b) avoids the chicken-and-egg problem of needing the CI user to deploy `CCETStorage-{Env}` while `CCETStorage-{Env}` must exist before the CI user IAM is valid. Pass the resulting `s3.IBucket` into `PrefixScopedGrant` as the `bucket` argument.
  - **Change**: restrict the CI user's S3 grants to:
    - `s3:*` on `arn:aws:s3:::ccet-{env}` and `arn:aws:s3:::ccet-{env}/*` (via `PrefixScopedGrant` with all four flags set so the CI user can deploy CDK assets, run smoke tests, and clean up test objects under the CCET-controlled bucket).
    - `s3:*` on `arn:aws:s3:::cdk-hnb659fds-assets-*` and `arn:aws:s3:::cdk-hnb659fds-assets-*/*` (CDK staging bucket — required for `cdk deploy`).
    - Explicitly NO access to `ccet-ml-datasets-*`, `ccet-ml-models-*`, `ccet-benchmark-reports-*`, `ccet`, `ccet-test` (the old buckets that will be deleted in Tasks 25/26 — denying write access makes Task 29.10's negative test meaningful).
  - **Verification step**: after the CI user IAM change is deployed, run `aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn <ci_user_arn> --action-names s3:PutObject --resource-arns arn:aws:s3:::ccet-ml-datasets-{env}/raw/probe.txt` and assert `EvalDecision=implicitDeny` (the removed grant results in implicit denial). This is evidence the negative test in Task 29.10 is measuring actual IAM behavior, not a false positive.
  - **Snapshots**: regenerate `cdk/ci_iam/` CDK snapshot tests.
  - *Design: "Post-Review Clarifications (Prompt 5)" § B2*

- [ ] 13a. Implement deploy-orchestrator migration pre-flight check (NEW per Prompt 4 A3, C5; revised per Prompt 5 A1 + C4)
  - **Task framing (per Prompt 5 C4)**: add a new pre-flight check step in the `cdk/deploy.py` deploy sequence, executed **before any stack deploy EXCEPT `CCETStorage-{Env}` itself** (the storage stack must be deployable before migration runs; otherwise there is no destination bucket). The implementer MAY either (a) extend the existing `_step_check_health` or (b) add a new private step method such as `_step_check_migration_sentinel`. Both are acceptable — the task does NOT prescribe a specific function name. Evidence (verified via `grepSearch`): `_step_check_health` exists at `cdk/deploy.py` line 336, but the choice of extension point is left to the implementer.
  - **Sentinel format — single canonical shape (per Prompt 5 A1)**: the pre-flight reads SSM parameter `/ccet/{env}/storage/migration-complete`. The value MUST parse as JSON matching the canonical shape defined in Req 18.4:
    ```json
    {"completed_at": "<ISO-8601>", "script_version": "<git-sha-or-tag>", "mapping_entries_verified": <int>}
    ```
    The pre-flight asserts the parsed JSON has a `completed_at` field of non-empty string type. Any non-JSON value, missing parameter, or missing `completed_at` fails the check with a `CCETDeploymentException` instructing the operator to run `python scripts/migrate_s3_storage.py --environment {env}`. **No legacy plain-string `"true"` value is accepted** — this parameter is introduced fresh in this spec and has no legacy consumers.
  - Add `--skip-migration-check` CLI flag (dest `ARG_SKIP_MIGRATION_CHECK`) that bypasses the pre-flight. Per Req 13.3 / Req 18.3: this flag MUST be implemented (not optional).
  - When `CCETStorage-{Env}` is the only stack being deployed (e.g., `--stacks CCETStorage-Dev`), the pre-flight MUST NOT trigger.
  - Write unit tests for all four paths:
    - (a) sentinel present and parseable with `completed_at` present → pre-flight passes;
    - (b) sentinel missing + no flag → `CCETDeploymentException` raised;
    - (c) sentinel present but NOT valid JSON (or JSON without `completed_at`) → `CCETDeploymentException` raised with a message distinguishing the parse failure from the missing-parameter case;
    - (d) sentinel missing + `--skip-migration-check` → pre-flight skipped.
  - *Design: "Risks and Mitigations" § Risk 5 mitigation, "Post-Review Clarifications (Prompt 4)" § A3, C5, "Post-Review Clarifications (Prompt 5)" § A1 + C4*
  - *Requirements: R13, R18*

- [ ] 29. **End-to-End Runtime Verification (NEW — Prompt 4 Task 29, gates Tasks 25 & 26)**

  > **Numbering note**: Task 29 is intentionally inserted between Task 24 (deploy + migrate) and Task 25 (legacy bucket deletion) — the tasks execute in order 1 → 2 → ... → 24 → **29** → 25 → 26 → 27 → 28. Task 29 is numbered 29 (not 25) to preserve the stable numbering of Tasks 25–28 across this spec revision.
  >
  > **GATE**: This task MUST complete with PASS before Task 25 (legacy bucket deletion) or Task 26 (old project bucket deletion) are permitted to run (Req 16). Any sub-task failure blocks bucket deletion until resolved and Task 29 is re-run end-to-end.
  >
  > This task is intentionally RUN-ONLY (it exercises live AWS resources). Every sub-task records its result in an evidence bundle at `tmp/evidence/e2e/{env}-{timestamp}/`. The bundle is the PASS/FAIL artifact.

  - [ ] 29.1 **Baseline capture** — record the state of the old and new buckets before verification begins.
    - `aws s3api list-objects-v2 --bucket ccet-ml-datasets-{env} --output json > tmp/evidence/e2e/{env}-{ts}/baseline-old-datasets.json`
    - Repeat for `ccet-ml-models-{env}` and `ccet-benchmark-reports-{env}`.
    - `aws s3api list-objects-v2 --bucket ccet-{env} --output json > tmp/evidence/e2e/{env}-{ts}/baseline-new.json`
    - These snapshots serve as the "zero-point" for per-prefix delta verification in 29.3–29.9.

  - [ ] 29.2 **DataCollector verification** — confirm the DataCollector Lambda writes to the new bucket's `raw/` prefix via Firehose.
    - Invoke the DataCollector Lambda directly (for one currency pair, e.g. `tBTCUSD`): `aws lambda invoke --function-name CCET-dev-DataCollector --payload '{"currency":"tBTCUSD","action":"collect_market_data"}' /tmp/out.json`.
    - Wait 70 seconds (Firehose buffer: 60s + 10s safety).
    - List objects under `s3://ccet-{env}/raw/year=.../month=.../day=.../currency=tBTCUSD/` with LastModified after the invoke timestamp. **Assert at least one object present.**
    - List objects under `s3://ccet-ml-datasets-{env}/raw/...` with LastModified after the invoke timestamp. **Assert zero objects** (old Firehose is decommissioned).

  - [ ] 29.3 **Raw archive Firehose verification** — confirm the CloudFormation `UpdateDestination` took effect.
    - `aws firehose describe-delivery-stream --delivery-stream-name CCET-{env}-RawDataArchive --query 'DeliveryStreamDescription.Destinations[0].ExtendedS3DestinationDescription.BucketARN'`.
    - **Assert** output equals `arn:aws:s3:::ccet-{env}`.

  - [ ] 29.4 **V1 pipeline verification** — DDB Streams → V1 Processing Lambda → V1 Firehose → `processed/v1-horizon2min-window30min/` on new bucket.
    - Query CloudWatch Logs for the V1 Processing Lambda (`/aws/lambda/ccet-data-processing-v1-{env}`) for the last 10 minutes — assert at least one successful invocation.
    - List objects under `s3://ccet-{env}/processed/v1-horizon2min-window30min/YYYY/MM/DD/HH/` with LastModified after Task 24 completion. **Assert at least one object present** (requires DataCollector to have run at least once — 29.2 ensures this).
    - List objects under `s3://ccet-ml-datasets-{env}/processed/v1-horizon2min-window30min/...` with LastModified after Task 24. **Assert zero new objects**.

  - [ ] 29.5 **V2 pipeline verification** — same as 29.4 but for V2.
    - V2 Processing Lambda (`/aws/lambda/ccet-data-processing-v2-{env}`) invocation confirmed in CloudWatch.
    - New-bucket path: `s3://ccet-{env}/processed/v2-horizon30min-window60min/YYYY/MM/DD/HH/` — at least one object.
    - Old-bucket path: `s3://ccet-ml-datasets-{env}/processed/v2-horizon30min-window60min/...` — zero new objects.

  - [ ] 29.6 **Decision engine verification** — Decision Lambda invokes successfully post-cutover and reads models from the new bucket.

    - For the DQN-dueling strategy: assert the log line indicating `s3://ccet-{env}/models/dqn/{version}/` (or equivalent) was accessed. Use CloudWatch Logs Insights query: `fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /s3:\\/\\/ccet-{env}\\/models\\/dqn/ | limit 10`.

    - Repeat for `ccet-ml-models-{env}` and `ccet-benchmark-reports-{env}`.

  - [ ] 29.11 **Negative test — HTTP (not HTTPS) access**: confirm SSL-only enforcement on new bucket.
    - **HTTPS probe (requires cleanup)**: Craft a signed PUT using `boto3` with `use_ssl=True` (default). Target `s3://ccet-{env}/temp/probe.txt`. **Assert success**, then delete the probe object — this is the ONLY probe that creates an object; cleanup applies to this path only.
    - **HTTP probe (NO cleanup required)**: Craft a signed PUT using `boto3` with a custom `use_ssl=False` session. Target the same `s3://ccet-{env}/temp/probe.txt`. **Assert the PUT is denied** — the assertion accepts EITHER `AccessDenied` (bucket policy with `aws:SecureTransport=false` deny) OR a TCP-level connection error / `EndpointConnectionError` (if AWS rejects the non-TLS connection entirely before policy evaluation — per Prompt 5 C3: boto3 with `use_ssl=False` connects to `http://s3.{region}.amazonaws.com`; if the endpoint refuses the TCP connection, a connection error is raised instead of a `ClientError`, and both outcomes prove the HTTP path is closed). The HTTP probe is denied, so **no object exists to clean up**.
    - *Requirements: R1.5 (SSL-only), R16*

    - Remediate (e.g., fix IAM, re-run migration script for a specific prefix, reconcile Firehose state).
    - Re-run the failed sub-task. If it passes, record the re-run evidence. Re-run Task 29.12 to update the bundle summary.

- [ ] 26. Retire old project buckets (AWS CLI procedure per C4 rewrite)
  > **GATE**: Only execute after Task 29 completes with PASS AND Task 25 is complete (Req 16).
  >
  > **Per Prompt 4 item C4**: Once Task 7/8/9 remove the bucket definitions from the CDK source, the three live buckets become "orphaned" — they persist physically but CloudFormation no longer manages them (per [AWS DeletionPolicy docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/TemplateReference/aws-attribute-deletionpolicy.html): *"If a resource is deleted, the `DeletionPolicy` retains the physical resource but ensures that it's deleted from CloudFormation's scope."*). A subsequent CDK PR that toggles `RemovalPolicy.DESTROY` + `auto_delete_objects=True` **cannot** delete them because they are no longer in any stack template. Deletion must therefore be done via AWS CLI.

  - [ ] 26.1 Empty and delete `ccet-ml-datasets-{env}` (versioning-enabled per drift D1 — requires explicit version deletion):
    ```bash
    # Profile is resolved from src.aws_config.AWSConfig.get_account(env).profile
    # per Prompt 5 D4 — NOT hardcoded bestehorn-learning (which is dev-only).
    # This makes the script reusable on stage and prod.
    ENV=dev
    # Resolve profile + region via Python helper (see scripts/delete_versioned_bucket.py below)
    PROFILE=$(python -c "from src.aws_config import aws_config; print(aws_config.get_account('${ENV}').profile)")
    REGION=$(python -c "from src.aws_config import aws_config; print(aws_config.get_account('${ENV}').region)")
    BUCKET=ccet-ml-datasets-${ENV}

    # Step 1: delete all object versions + delete markers
    # Paginate list-object-versions and batch-delete up to 1000 at a time
    aws --profile $PROFILE --region $REGION s3api list-object-versions \
        --bucket $BUCKET \
        --output json \
        --query '{Objects: Versions[].{Key:Key,VersionId:VersionId}}' \
        > /tmp/versions.json
    aws --profile $PROFILE --region $REGION s3api delete-objects \
        --bucket $BUCKET \
        --delete file:///tmp/versions.json

    aws --profile $PROFILE --region $REGION s3api list-object-versions \
        --bucket $BUCKET \
        --output json \
        --query '{Objects: DeleteMarkers[].{Key:Key,VersionId:VersionId}}' \
        > /tmp/markers.json
    aws --profile $PROFILE --region $REGION s3api delete-objects \
        --bucket $BUCKET \
        --delete file:///tmp/markers.json

    # Step 2: remove the bucket itself
    aws --profile $PROFILE --region $REGION s3 rb s3://$BUCKET
    ```
    Wrap the version-delete loop in a Python helper `scripts/delete_versioned_bucket.py` that takes `--environment` (required), resolves profile + region via `src.aws_config.AWSConfig.get_account(env)` (per Prompt 5 D4 — no hardcoded profile), accepts `--bucket` + `--dry-run`, and drives the pagination + batch-delete loop. Commit the helper as part of this task so stage/prod rollouts (Task 27) are repeatable with no script edits between environments.
  - [ ] 26.2 Empty and delete `ccet-ml-models-{env}` — same version-delete procedure (drift D2 confirms versioning=Enabled here too).
  - [ ] 26.3 Empty and delete `ccet-benchmark-reports-{env}` — versioning is NOT enabled here per `docs/s3-storage-structure.md`, so `aws s3 rm --recursive s3://ccet-benchmark-reports-{env}` + `aws s3 rb s3://ccet-benchmark-reports-{env}` is sufficient.
  - [ ] 26.4 Confirm the three old buckets no longer exist: `aws s3api list-buckets --query 'Buckets[?Name==`ccet-ml-datasets-dev` || Name==`ccet-ml-models-dev` || Name==`ccet-benchmark-reports-dev`]'` returns empty list.
  - [ ] 26.5 **Unit-test the `scripts/delete_versioned_bucket.py` helper (NEW per Prompt 6 B3)**: write `test/scripts/test_delete_versioned_bucket.py` that mocks `boto3.client('s3')` and asserts: (a) `--dry-run` makes no `delete-objects` or `s3 rb` calls; (b) the pagination loop handles > 1000 versions correctly (simulate two pages); (c) profile + region are resolved via `src.aws_config.AWSConfig.get_account(env)` — not hardcoded; (d) non-versioned bucket (`--bucket ccet-benchmark-reports-{env}`) falls back to `rm --recursive` + `rb`. Coverage for this module is included in the Task 28.7 assertion.
  - *Design: "Sequence Diagrams" § "Phase 1 Deployment Sequence" step "aws s3 rb --force", "Risks and Mitigations" § Risk 7 (C4), "Post-Review Clarifications (Prompt 4)" § C4*
  - *Requirements: R9, R16*

Model: # Fourth-Pass Critical Review

## A. Execution Blockers

### A1. Correctness Property 5 text still contradicts Req 1.2 and Task 22

Requirements.md Req 1.2 says AWS-default AES256 is "acceptable and expected" and the smoke test must only forbid `KmsKeyId`/`KmsMasterKeyID`.

Task 22's `smoke_test_no_encryption` and the Testing Strategy paragraph both now correctly say "Do NOT assert `ServerSideEncryptionConfigurationNotFoundError`".

**But design.md's Correctness Property 5 contains this (self-contradictory) text**:
> "CDK synth output has no explicit `BucketEncryption.KmsKeyId` or `KmsMasterKeyID` on the consolidated bucket. At runtime, AWS automatically applies SSE-S3 (AES256)…"

That text is correct at runtime, but the property is labeled "**No-encryption invariant**" — which is misleading since the bucket IS encrypted with SSE-S3 at runtime. This mirrors the C1 nit from my prior review that was marked "nice to fix" but never fixed. If Kiro implements a property test named `test_no_encryption_invariant` based on this property's title alone, the test will fail on every new bucket.

**Fix**: rename Correctness Property 5 from "No-encryption invariant" to "No-customer-KMS invariant" (or similar). This was a nit in the previous pass but has now become relevant because Task 2.1's tests will likely derive their test names from the property names.

### A2. `scripts/delete_versioned_bucket.py` is referenced before Task 26.5 creates it

Task 9a (sub-bullet "Bucket import mechanism") references the helper. Task 26.1 uses it. Task 27 (stage/prod) uses it. Task 28.7 asserts coverage for it.

**But the first task that creates the helper is Task 26.5 itself** — which runs AFTER Task 26.1 and Task 26.2 (which use the helper).

Re-reading carefully: Task 26.1 provides a bash script that calls `aws` directly (works without the helper) and includes the text "*Wrap the version-delete loop in a Python helper `scripts/delete_versioned_bucket.py` …*" — so Task 26.1 does implicitly create the helper before using it on 26.2. But:

- **Task 26.5** is labeled "Unit-test the helper" — it tests the helper but does not explicitly create it.
- The task ordering suggests the helper is created inline during Task 26.1 execution, tested in Task 26.5, and reused in 26.2/27.

This is an ambiguity Kiro will likely resolve by creating the helper in Task 26.1 (OK), but could also resolve by deferring creation to Task 26.5 (NOT OK — 26.1 and 26.2 would fail).

**Fix**: promote helper creation to a dedicated sub-bullet:
- `26.0` (new): Create `scripts/delete_versioned_bucket.py` with the described CLI interface + pagination loop + dry-run support.
- `26.1`: use the helper to delete `ccet-ml-datasets-{env}`.
- `26.2`: use the helper for `ccet-ml-models-{env}`.
- `26.5`: unit-test the helper (keep as-is).

### A3. Task 9 (benchmarking EventBridge update) — the Metrics Lambda handler wrapper is not explicitly updated

Task 9's new EventBridge bullet says "configure `events_targets.LambdaFunction(..., event=events.RuleTargetInput.from_object({..., 'ssm_base_path': …}))`" — this is the CDK-side change.

Task 16's matching runtime side says `report_generator.py` itself does NOT read SSM; its caller (the "Metrics Lambda handler") extracts `ssm_base_path` from the event and passes it down.

**Gap**: no task explicitly updates the Metrics Lambda handler (`src/lambdas/benchmark_metrics/handler.py` per the project description) to extract `ssm_base_path` from `event` and call `get_ssm_param_path` → `ssm.get_parameter`. Task 16 describes only the `report_generator.py` signature change.

If Kiro reads Task 16 literally, `report_generator.py` gets a new `bucket_name` parameter but no caller is updated to pass it. The pipeline breaks at runtime.

**Fix**: extend Task 16 (or add a new Task 16a) to explicitly update the Metrics Lambda handler that invokes `write_report_to_s3`. Name the file path — based on the project description it is `src/lambdas/benchmark_metrics/handler.py`.

Analogous concern exists for Task 11's Step Functions ssm_base_path injection — Tasks 12 and 13 do specify that their handlers extract from the event, so those are OK.

### A4. Task 4 enables the CI guardrail (Task 23) on code that Task 4 just deleted

Task 4 says "Verify no consumer still imports the removed fields: `grep -rn "ml_datasets_bucket_name\|ml_models_bucket_name" src/ cdk/ scripts/ test/` — expect matches only in test files that are updated in the same PR."

But the CI guardrail in Task 23 forbids the strings `ccet-ml-datasets-`, `ccet-ml-models-`, `ccet-benchmark-reports-` — **not** `ml_datasets_bucket_name` or `ml_models_bucket_name`. These are different strings.

The Python field names `ml_datasets_bucket_name` don't contain hyphens or `ccet-` prefixes. They would **not** trip the CI guardrail. This is actually fine — but the logic chain described in Task 4 ("deprecated aliases would conflict with the CI guardrail in Task 23") is wrong. The deprecated aliases would not conflict with the CI guardrail because field names don't contain the forbidden strings.

**Impact**: the stated rationale for "delete the old fields immediately" is incorrect. The actual reason for deleting them is good hygiene, but Task 4's justification argument does not hold. Kiro might conclude the prohibition against deprecated aliases is erroneous and keep them.

**Fix**: correct Task 4's rationale. The aliases should still be deleted (because mid-migration same-PR consumer updates cover the breakage), but not because of the CI guardrail. Or alternatively: if aliases are kept, their **values** (`"ccet-ml-datasets-dev"` etc.) would trip the CI guardrail, which is the actual correct reasoning.

## C. Clarifications

### C1. Req 3.1 is now self-referential (two-layer "both views are consistent" argument)

Req 3.1 enumerates 10 prefix paths but says 9 top-level categories, and Correctness Property 10 says 9. The requirement text tries to reconcile both, ending with a paragraph explaining they agree.

This works technically. But a smoke test implementing "Req 3.1" will have to choose which list (10 vs 9) to iterate over. The Req text says "Smoke tests implementing Req 3.2 SHOULD enforce the 10-path form" — but Task 22's `smoke_test_prefix_taxonomy_enforced` doesn't actually enumerate prefixes at all; it just tests one bogus prefix.

**No fix needed** — the smoke test for Req 3.2 does not need to enumerate. But Req 3.1's "both views are consistent" paragraph is more complicated than needed. Future spec readers will be confused.

**Minor fix (optional)**: simplify Req 3.1 to list exactly the 10 paths without invoking Correctness Property 10's 9-category count, OR update Correctness Property 10 to list 10 paths (tautologically consistent).

### C2. Task 9a's IAM-simulation verification step can silently pass even if the grant is wrong

Task 9a's verification step says:
> "run `aws iam simulate-principal-policy ...` and assert `EvalDecision=implicitDeny`"

But `implicitDeny` is the default state for any action against any resource NOT explicitly allowed. Even if the CI user still has `s3:*` on `*` but the policy is applied to a DIFFERENT IAM role than the one being simulated, the result could still be `implicitDeny` — a false positive.

**Fix**: add a positive-control assertion too: run `simulate-principal-policy` against `arn:aws:s3:::ccet-dev/raw/probe.txt` (the new bucket) and assert `EvalDecision=allowed` (the grant is in place). Combined with the negative assertion, this proves the policy is correctly scoped.

### C3. Task 11's "Step Functions ssm_base_path injection" wording vs. current implementation

Task 11 says use `sfn_tasks.LambdaInvoke` with a `payload` that merges incoming input + injected field. Looking at the project description, the existing RL Training Pipeline uses `aws_stepfunctions_tasks.SageMakerCreateTrainingJob` for training but the Lambda invocations (data export, registration) use `LambdaInvoke`. Confirming this is reasonable but not verified in the spec.

**Fix (optional)**: cite `cdk/rl_training_pipeline/stack.py` line number where the `LambdaInvoke` tasks are defined, so Kiro modifies the right place and doesn't accidentally try to patch the `SageMakerCreateTrainingJob` task.

### C4. `MIGRATION_MAPPING` import from `scripts/` is nonstandard

Task 20 says: "Import `MIGRATION_MAPPING` from `scripts/migrate_s3_storage.py`".

Python's standard practice treats `scripts/` as CLI entry points, not importable modules. `scripts/__init__.py` may not exist. `sys.path` manipulation may be needed. Tests for `scripts/update_model_registry_bucket.py` (Task 20.1) would need to handle this.

**Fix**: extract `MIGRATION_MAPPING` to a shared module that both scripts import, e.g. `src/migrations/mappings.py` or `scripts/_shared/mappings.py` (making `_shared` importable via an `__init__.py`). Alternatively, declare in Task 20 that both scripts locally define the mapping with a "MUST match byte-for-byte" comment — lower quality but simpler.

### C5. Task 24.4 sentinel write happens inside `migrate_s3_storage.py` but operator visibility is unclear

Task 24.4 says "On success, the script writes `/ccet/dev/storage/migration-complete` SSM sentinel (Req 7.6)."

The operator has no way to verify this from the task's checklist. Task 24.5 inspects the JSON report but not the SSM parameter.

**Fix (minor)**: add to Task 24.5 an explicit check: `aws --profile {profile} ssm get-parameter --name /ccet/{env}/storage/migration-complete` and confirm the JSON has `completed_at` and `mapping_entries_verified`. This catches the case where the migration script completes but the SSM write silently fails.

The feature that is getting implemented here is irrelevant and not important, but the process is: We start with a general idea and a discussion about gaps and questions, which leads to an initial prompt for the feature being passed to Kiro in specification mode (not vibe coding). Kiro then generates a set of initial spec files and then I have to manually copy&paste these spec files back for review to the reviewing agent/entity, copy&paste the result of the review back to kiro to generate a new set of spec files etc. until the specs are ready for implementation and the review finds no more issues. Model: # Designing the Spec-Review Agent

## My Understanding of the Goal

You want a Kiro CLI custom agent that replaces the manual copy-paste loop you just went through four times. The agent should:

1. **Receive** an initial idea (plus optionally: a discussion, an initial prompt, or existing spec files).
2. **Drive** the generation of the initial spec files (or accept them if Kiro has already produced them).
3. **Review** the resulting spec files (`requirements.md`, `design.md`, `tasks.md`, maybe `prompts.md`) using MCP documentation servers, web research for best-practice patterns, and inspection of the actual codebase.
4. **Feed review findings back** to cause the specs to be updated.
5. **Loop** until the specs are ready for implementation.
6. **Terminate** with a final artifact — the polished, ready-to-implement spec files + an evidence bundle documenting every review cycle, every fix, and every source of evidence.

The agent must be **language-agnostic** and **project-agnostic** — the fact that the example was AWS/CDK/Python is irrelevant to the agent's design.

Architecturally, this agent fits the same mold as your Documentation Deficit Resolver and CI Coverage Resolver: state directory under `.kiro/agent-state/`, resume-state mechanism, No-Guessing Rule, No-Shortcuts Mandate, Non-Interruption Mandate, evidence ledger, and explicit anti-patterns.

Before drafting the prompt, I have several questions that determine the agent's fundamental shape. These group into five clusters.

---

## Cluster 1 — How the Agent Integrates with Kiro Spec Generation

This is the most important question and determines everything else.

**Q1.1** — When the agent needs the specs to be updated in response to review findings, how does the update happen? Three plausible models:

- **(a) Agent-as-editor**: the custom agent directly edits the spec files itself. It reads them, reviews them, applies the edits it identified. No separate "Kiro spec mode" is involved during iteration. (Simplest; but you explicitly said your current workflow is *not* vibe coding — Kiro's spec mode is distinct and has value.)

- **(b) Agent-as-driver**: the custom agent invokes a separate Kiro spec session as a subprocess (e.g., `kiro spec update --feature ... --feedback-file ...`), passing the review findings and letting Kiro's spec mode do the actual editing. The custom agent only reviews and gates.

- **(c) Hybrid**: the agent generates review findings as a file that the user (or a wrapper script) feeds to Kiro spec mode. The custom agent then re-reads the updated files and reviews again.

Which of these matches how Kiro CLI actually exposes spec mode? Is there a `kiro spec` subcommand or equivalent that can be invoked non-interactively with a feedback file? If not, model (a) is the only viable one — and the agent effectively becomes both reviewer and editor.

**Q1.2** — Does the initial spec generation (idea → v1 of requirements/design/tasks) also happen inside this agent, or is v1 produced in a separate Kiro spec session before the agent is invoked?

My recommendation would be to scope the agent as the **iterative review loop only** — it accepts an initial spec version (v1) as input and returns the terminal spec version. The initial generation remains a separate, interactive Kiro spec session because that step typically benefits from the user's involvement in answering open questions. If you want the agent to also handle v1 generation, that's a larger scope.

## Cluster 2 — Loop Termination

**Q2.1** — You observed in the example that "each pass introduces ~5 small errors" and convergence does not reach zero. Given this empirical reality, what is the correct termination condition?

- **(a) Zero execution-blockers** (A-severity issues only) — accept some B/C/D-severity issues as cost of shipping. In the example, this was met after pass 3.
- **(b) Zero execution-blockers AND zero user-intent deviations** (A + B) — stricter. Met after pass 4 with the 7 must-fix list.
- **(c) Zero issues of any severity** — likely never converges and risks thrashing.
- **(d) Fixed iteration budget** (e.g., 5 passes max) with the best-available state delivered at the end.
- **(e) Some combination**: terminate on (a) OR (d), whichever comes first.

My recommendation is **(e)**: terminate when an iteration produces zero A-severity findings AND zero B-severity findings, OR when a hard iteration cap (e.g., 6) is reached. The cap prevents the thrashing you noted.

**Q2.2** — Should the agent ever escalate to the user? For example, when a review finding requires a product decision (your "Option a / Option b" prompts in the example), the human's input is genuinely needed. Three choices:

- **(a) Fully autonomous**: the agent resolves all ambiguity by its best research-backed judgment and records the decision in the evidence ledger. The user reviews at the end.
- **(b) Selective user-input**: the agent pauses (via `userInput` tool) when a decision is a product/business matter that research cannot resolve (e.g., "indefinite retention vs. 180-day expiration"). All other findings resolved autonomously.
- **(c) Fully interactive**: every iteration pauses for user confirmation.

Given your other agents' Non-Interruption Mandate style, and that you explicitly said the goal is to eliminate the manual copy-paste, I'd recommend **(a)** with a narrow carve-out for truly un-researchable product decisions. But this needs your preference.

## Cluster 3 — Review Scope and Evidence

**Q3.1** — Which evidence sources should the agent use? Your list in the initial question implied three:

- **MCP documentation servers** (AWS docs, CDK docs, library-specific servers).
- **Web research for patterns** (this requires a web-search MCP server or equivalent tool).
- **The actual project codebase** (read files, grep, inspect existing patterns).

Are all three definitely in scope, and do you have concrete MCP servers available for each? Specifically, is there a web-search MCP server in your Kiro setup, or should the agent rely only on MCP documentation servers + codebase inspection?

**Q3.2** — How deep should the codebase inspection go? Options:

- **(a) Lightweight**: grep for symbols mentioned in the spec, verify they exist.
- **(b) Medium**: (a) plus read files around cited line numbers to verify the spec's claims about existing code.
- **(c) Deep**: (b) plus pattern mining — for each design decision, find analogous patterns elsewhere in the codebase and check consistency.

The example review clearly did (b) in places ("verified via grepSearch that `_step_check_health` exists at `cdk/deploy.py:336`"). I'd recommend **(b)** as the default with **(c)** escalation when a finding alleges inconsistency with existing patterns.

**Q3.3** — Does the agent need to verify that tests exist and pass before termination, or is spec-readiness strictly about the spec files themselves? The example's final verdict was about spec readiness, not about running implementation. I assume the agent stops at spec readiness (does NOT invoke any implementation or test execution).

## Cluster 4 — Input/Output Contract

**Q4.1** — What does the agent receive as input? Concretely:

- The feature name / spec directory path (e.g., `.kiro/specs/my-feature/`).
- The initial spec files (`requirements.md`, `design.md`, `tasks.md`).
- Optionally, a discussion document or initial prompt that captures the user's intent (the analog of `prompts/StorageDiscussion.txt` in the example).

Is there a canonical layout that every project of yours already follows for this? If yes, the agent can detect the spec directory; if no, the agent needs explicit pointers.

**Q4.2** — What does the agent produce as output?

- The updated spec files (in place).
- A review-session bundle at `.kiro/agent-state/spec-reviewer-agent/session-{timestamp}/` containing: per-iteration review findings, per-iteration fix record, evidence ledger, MCP lookup transcripts, codebase-grep transcripts, final verdict.
- A terminal summary report (stdout/final message) describing what was changed, what sources were consulted, and any user-decision points that were (or were not) resolved.

Does this match what you want, or should the agent write updates only when a "commit now" signal is given?

## Cluster 5 — Agent-Specific Behavior

**Q5.1** — Should the review emulate the same 4-layer structure your manual reviewer used (Execution Blockers / Gaps / Errors / Clarifications / Minor Nits)? This is a strong pattern and already produces actionable output.

**Q5.2** — The example review had explicit references like `A1`, `B2`, `C3`. Should the agent preserve this taxonomy across iterations, or regenerate IDs each iteration? Preserving them across iterations aids traceability but complicates the review logic (some findings disappear, new ones appear).

**Q5.3** — Does the agent need to maintain a "prompts.md" change log (verbatim prompts + answers + userInput decisions) matching the pattern you use? This is a significant artifact in your example workflow.

---

## Proposed Path Forward

Once you answer the above, I'll draft the prompt in the same structural pattern as your existing agents:

- **Role and Identity** — spec-review-and-iterate agent
- **Conventions** — `the state directory`, `the spec directory`, `the evidence bundle`
- **Mission Statement** — reach a ready-to-implement spec via iterative review
- **The Non-Interruption Mandate** — adapted for this agent (with your Q2.2 answer driving the carve-outs)
- **The No-Shortcuts Mandate** — no superficial review, no fake convergence
- **The No-Guessing Rule** — every finding cites MCP doc, codebase line, or web source
- **Hard Constraints** — no code edits outside spec files, mandatory MCP verification, mandatory codebase verification
- **Discovery Phase** — resume-state check, spec-directory discovery, MCP-server enumeration, codebase inventory
- **The Main Loop** — Review → Classify → Update → Re-review, with termination per Q2.1
- **Termination Report** — final readiness verdict + evidence bundle citation

My strong preference is to converge on Q1.1 first (how the agent integrates with Kiro's spec mode) because it fundamentally shapes the rest. If Kiro CLI doesn't expose a non-interactive spec-update command, the agent becomes model (a) — the reviewer-and-editor — and the prompt becomes substantially simpler.

What are your answers to these clusters?

# User Answers to Open Items

This section records the user's answers to the clusters of open questions posed at the end of the discussion above. Entries are added cluster-by-cluster as answers are collected.

## Cluster 1 — Kiro spec-mode integration (RESOLVED)

### Q1.1 — How does the agent cause the specs to change in response to review findings?

**Answer: Model (c) — Hybrid, agent-as-reviewer.**

The agent:
- Reads the spec files from `.kiro/specs/<topic>/`.
- Performs the critical review using MCP documentation servers, web research, and codebase inspection.
- Writes the review findings to a file in the same spec directory.
- The user feeds that file to Kiro IDE's spec mode to update the spec files.
- The user re-invokes the agent to review the updated specs.
- Loop until the review finds no blocking issues.

The agent does NOT directly edit `requirements.md`, `design.md`, or `tasks.md`. It writes only review-finding files into the spec directory plus its own state under `.kiro/agent-state/<agent-name>/`.

Rationale beyond automating copy-paste: the agent has access to MCP documentation servers, internet resources, and the project codebase, allowing it to verify the spec against best practices and existing patterns — capabilities the manual review process does not have.

### Q1.2 — Does the agent also generate the v1 prompt from a blank idea?

**Answer: Yes, but via a separate agent — two-agent architecture.**

The full lifecycle splits into two phases, each handled by its own agent:

**Phase A — Spec Prompt Authoring (interactive with user).**
- Handled by a dedicated `spec-prompt-author-agent`.
- The user invokes the agent with a blank or minimal idea.
- The agent asks clarifying questions, performs research (MCP servers, web, codebase), and converges with the user on a well-formed initial prompt for Kiro IDE's spec mode.
- Phase A is inherently interactive. The Non-Interruption Mandate does NOT apply here in the same form as it does for autonomous agents; interviewing the user is the agent's job.

**Manual step** — the user feeds the authored prompt to Kiro IDE. Kiro IDE's spec mode generates `requirements.md`, `design.md`, `tasks.md` in the spec directory.

**Phase B — Spec Review Loop (autonomous per iteration).**
- Handled by a dedicated `spec-review-agent`.
- The user points the agent at `.kiro/specs/<topic>/`.
- The agent reviews the spec files and writes a review-iteration file.
- The user feeds the review back to Kiro IDE to update the specs.
- The user re-invokes the agent for the next iteration.
- Loop until the agent's review finds no blocking issues.
- Phase B follows the standard autonomous-agent pattern (Non-Interruption Mandate, No-Shortcuts Mandate, No-Guessing Rule).

**Why two agents instead of one two-mode agent:** Phase A's "interview the user" behavior is fundamentally different from Phase B's "operate autonomously" behavior. Mixing them in a single prompt would weaken both the Non-Interruption Mandate (critical for Phase B) and the interview flow (critical for Phase A). Each agent stays small, focused, and matches the house style of existing agents (`doc-reviewer-agent`, `dead-code-removal-agent`).

### File naming and directory conventions

All artifacts live under `.kiro/specs/<topic>/` alongside Kiro IDE's generated spec files. The `prompts/` directory convention is retired.

**Phase A (Spec Prompt Author agent) writes:**
- `prompt.md` — the final initial prompt for Kiro IDE spec mode (the artifact handed to Kiro IDE).
- `prompt-discussion.md` — verbatim Q&A log between the user and the agent, providing a traceable record of why the prompt looks the way it does.

**Phase B (Spec Review agent) writes:**
- `review-iteration-01.md`, `review-iteration-02.md`, ... — one file per review cycle. This matches how the user currently copy-pastes a review into the Kiro IDE manually. One-file-per-iteration makes each review self-contained and easy to feed back to Kiro IDE.
- `review-log.md` — running summary of iterations and convergence status across the loop.

**Agent state directories (separate from spec directories):**
- `.kiro/agent-state/spec-prompt-author-agent/<session-id>/` — Phase A session state.
- `.kiro/agent-state/spec-review-agent/<session-id>/` — Phase B session state, including evidence ledger, MCP lookup transcripts, codebase-grep transcripts.



## Cluster 2 — Loop termination and user escalation (RESOLVED)

This cluster applies to the Phase B `spec-review-agent` only. Phase A's termination is natural (it ends when `prompt.md` has been authored and saved).

### Q2.1 — Termination condition for the review loop

**Answer: Convergence-and-effort model, no hard iteration cap.**

The agent's per-invocation termination logic:

1. Perform the review of the current spec files.
2. Classify findings by severity:
   - **A** — Execution blockers (spec cannot be implemented as written).
   - **B** — User-intent deviations (spec implementable but deviates from stated user intent).
   - **C** — Clarifications / risks / under-specified areas.
   - **D** — Minor nits (style, wording, formatting).
3. Maintain a persistent counter `consecutive_clean_AB` in the agent's state directory:
   - If the current review has any A or B finding: reset `consecutive_clean_AB = 0`.
   - Else: `consecutive_clean_AB += 1`.
4. Track the C+D total across recent invocations to detect stuck states.
5. Emit one of three verdicts in the review-iteration file:

   - **READY** — `consecutive_clean_AB >= 5` AND `C == 0` AND `D == 0`.
     The spec is ready for implementation. No further review invocations are needed.

   - **READY-WITH-MINOR-DEFICITS** — `consecutive_clean_AB >= 5` AND (`C > 0` OR `D > 0`) AND the combined C+D count has not decreased across the last 3 invocations.
     The spec is implementable. Residual C/D items are listed with the evidence trail showing why they could not be resolved through best-practices research (MCP, documentation, codebase patterns). The user reviews and either accepts the residual items or provides guidance.

   - **NOT-READY** — any other state. The review file lists all A/B/C/D findings with evidence.

6. The agent never terminates the loop unilaterally — it emits a verdict and the user decides whether to re-invoke. READY and READY-WITH-MINOR-DEFICITS are signals that further invocation is unnecessary.

**Rationale:**
- No hard iteration cap — the user wants the agent to spend effort on minor deficits when it can make progress.
- The minimum-5 clean-of-A/B threshold prevents premature termination before convergence stability is established.
- The C+D stuck-counter prevents infinite loops on minor deficits that cannot be resolved through research.
- The agent MUST focus its effort on using MCP documentation servers, web research, and codebase inspection to resolve C/D findings — not merely list them.

### Q2.2 — Should the agent escalate product decisions to the user?

**Answer: (b) — Selective user input via structured review-file sections, with mandatory self-resolution attempts first.**

Hard rules governing user escalation:

1. **Self-resolution is mandatory before escalation.** The agent MUST attempt to resolve every question through:
   - MCP documentation servers (AWS, CDK, library-specific).
   - Web research for applicable best practices and patterns.
   - Codebase inspection for existing patterns, conventions, and coding guidelines.
   
   Delegating a question to the user without a documented self-resolution attempt is an anti-pattern and is explicitly forbidden.

2. **Only genuine product/business decisions may be escalated.** When research genuinely cannot settle a question (e.g., business preferences, organizational priorities, compliance requirements not documented in the codebase), the agent presents:
   - A clear statement of the question.
   - **Multiple well-reasoned options**, each with evidence (MCP citations, codebase references, best-practice sources).
   - The agent's recommended option with explicit rationale.
   - The consequences of each option for the spec and the downstream implementation.

3. **No runtime pauses.** The agent never pauses execution waiting for user input. Open questions surface as a structured section in the review-iteration file (e.g., `## Open Product Decisions`). The agent proceeds to the end of the review within a single invocation.

4. **Persistence of resolutions.** When the user resolves an open question (by providing guidance that Kiro IDE then incorporates into the specs), the question and its resolution are recorded persistently in the spec directory (e.g., appended to `prompt-discussion.md` or a dedicated `open-questions.md`) so that:
   - A session crash or restart does not lose the resolution.
   - Future review iterations can reference the resolution as authoritative evidence.
   - The historical record of product decisions remains traceable alongside the spec.

5. **Escalation does not block termination.** The presence of open questions does not by itself prevent a READY or READY-WITH-MINOR-DEFICITS verdict, as long as the A/B/C/D severity criteria are met. Open questions are metadata about product decisions, not deficits in the spec itself.



## Cluster 3 — Review scope and evidence (RESOLVED)

### Q3.1 — Evidence sources

**Answer: All three evidence sources are in scope for BOTH agents (Phase A prompt-author and Phase B reviewer).**

Required evidence sources:

1. **MCP documentation servers** — AWS documentation MCP, AWS CDK MCP, and any other MCP documentation servers available in the current Kiro session (language-specific, library-specific, framework-specific). Both agents MUST enumerate available MCP servers during their Discovery Phase and use them to verify external-technology claims.

2. **Web research** — targeted web searches for best-practice patterns, community conventions, framework recommendations, and authoritative third-party documentation for topics not covered by available MCP servers. Both agents MUST use web research when MCP coverage is insufficient.

3. **Project codebase** — read access to the project's source code, tests, configuration, and existing documentation. Both agents MUST inspect the codebase for existing patterns, coding conventions, architectural decisions, and project-specific guidelines (e.g., content under `.kiro/steering/`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, existing modules in `src/`/`cdk/`, existing test patterns in `test/`).

The rationale for giving Phase A the same evidence access is that the prompt-author agent needs it to:
- Ask informed clarifying questions grounded in the project's actual state.
- Propose specific technical choices in the authored prompt based on existing patterns and documented best practices.
- Avoid producing a prompt that contradicts project conventions or proposes reinvention of existing components.

### Q3.2 — Codebase inspection depth

**Answer: Deep inspection, including pattern mining.**

For every design decision in the spec (Phase B) or every technical choice being authored into the prompt (Phase A), the agent MUST:

1. **Verify symbol existence** — grep/search for symbols, modules, and paths the spec references and confirm they exist.
2. **Read cited code** — for every file or line the spec cites, read the relevant section to verify the spec's claims about the code's behavior, interface, or structure.
3. **Pattern mining** — locate analogous patterns elsewhere in the codebase for each non-trivial design decision. Flag any inconsistency between the proposed design and existing conventions as a finding. Examples:
   - If the spec proposes a new CDK construct pattern, check how existing stacks handle similar cases.
   - If the spec proposes a new error-handling approach, check existing error handling in comparable modules.
   - If the spec proposes file or module layout, check the project's existing layout conventions.
   - If the spec proposes testing patterns, check how comparable features are tested elsewhere.

**Rationale from the user:** "I would rather spend more effort on aligning the spec and resulting code with the best practices and the existing code base rather than reimplementations or ambiguity as well as duplicated work."

Corollary rules:

- **Duplication detection is a primary concern.** If the spec proposes functionality that already exists in the codebase (or closely resembles existing functionality), this is a finding. The spec MUST either reuse the existing component, extend it explicitly, or document why a new parallel implementation is justified.
- **Convention deviations MUST be justified.** If the spec proposes a pattern that differs from existing codebase conventions, the deviation itself is a finding. The spec MUST include explicit rationale for the deviation, or conform to the existing convention.
- **Project-specific steering documents are authoritative.** Content under `.kiro/steering/`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `CODING_GUIDELINES.md`, and similar governance documents is treated as first-class evidence. A spec that violates documented project rules is a finding regardless of what external best practices say.

### Q3.3 — Does the agent run tests or implementation tooling?

**Answer: (a) — Spec readiness only. No test execution, no implementation tooling beyond read-only inspection.**

The agent is active **before** implementation begins. Running the test suite, invoking linters, type checkers, or any tooling that changes project state is out of scope. Permitted operations are limited to:

- Reading files (source, tests, documentation, configuration).
- Static search (grep, ripgrep, file globbing) across the repository.
- MCP documentation server queries.
- Web searches.
- Reading git metadata (`git log`, `git blame`) for historical context — read-only only.

Forbidden operations:
- Running the project's test suite.
- Running linters, formatters, type checkers, or any tool that could modify files.
- Installing dependencies.
- Invoking any build or deployment command.
- Creating git commits or branches.
- Any network operation beyond MCP server queries and web research.

Running tests and verifying implementation is the job of the implementation agents (e.g., `dead-code-removal-agent`) and Kiro IDE itself during and after implementation. The spec-review agent's scope ends at producing a READY verdict.



## Cluster 4 — Input / Output contract (RESOLVED)

### Q4.1 — Invocation inputs

**Phase A (`spec-prompt-author-agent`) — Option (d), preference toward (a).**

The agent accepts any of:
- **No arguments** (preferred) — the agent asks "what shall we call this topic?" as its first question, then asks for the seed idea. The topic answer becomes the directory name under `.kiro/specs/`.
- **Topic name only** — e.g., `--topic storage-refactor`. The agent creates `.kiro/specs/storage-refactor/` and asks for the seed idea.
- **Topic name + seed text or seed file** — the agent uses the seed as the starting point for its clarification questions instead of starting cold.

Adaptation rules:
- If no topic is provided, asking for the topic name is the agent's **first** interview question. The directory is created immediately after the user answers, and all subsequent Phase A output lands there.
- Directory names MUST be slugified from the user's answer (lowercase, hyphens, alphanumeric only). If the slugified name collides with an existing directory under `.kiro/specs/`, the agent asks the user to disambiguate rather than silently overwriting or appending a suffix.
- No `_draft-<timestamp>/` convention — the directory is always named after the confirmed topic.

**Phase B (`spec-review-agent`) — Option (a), explicit path required, with disambiguation fallback.**

The agent accepts:
- **Spec directory path** — e.g., `--spec-dir .kiro/specs/storage-refactor/` (the primary and preferred form).

If the invocation is ambiguous or unclear about which spec is being reviewed, the agent asks the user to point at the correct spec directory as a one-time clarification. This is the single permitted interactive question for the Phase B agent; it happens before the Discovery Phase, not during the review loop. Once the directory is identified, the agent operates fully autonomously for the remainder of the invocation.

Auto-detection by scanning `.kiro/specs/` and picking the most recent directory is NOT permitted — it risks operating on the wrong spec.

### Q4.2 — Outputs

**Phase A outputs (written to disk at termination):**

Under `.kiro/specs/<topic>/`:
- `prompt.md` — the final initial prompt for Kiro IDE spec mode. Self-contained and hand-off ready.
- `prompt-discussion.md` — verbatim Q&A log between user and agent, providing the traceable record of prompt derivation.

Under `.kiro/agent-state/spec-prompt-author-agent/<session-id>/`:
- `resume_state.md`
- `iteration_log.md`
- `evidence_ledger.md`
- `mcp_transcripts.md`
- `web_research_log.md`
- `codebase_inspection_log.md`

Final chat message: confirms `prompt.md` is ready, points at the file path, and indicates the user's next step (feed `prompt.md` to Kiro IDE spec mode).

**Phase B outputs (written per invocation):**

Under `.kiro/specs/<topic>/`:
- `review-iteration-NN.md` — the current review, zero-padded two-digit iteration number (`01`, `02`, ..., `99`). Persistent history, never overwritten.
- `review-latest.md` — stable alias, overwritten at the end of every invocation to be byte-identical to the most recent `review-iteration-NN.md`. This is the file the user points Kiro IDE at with "here is the feedback on the spec, work on this accordingly."
- `review-log.md` — append-only running summary with one line per iteration: timestamp, iteration number, verdict, A/B/C/D counts, `consecutive_clean_AB`.
- `open-questions.md` — created or updated when the current iteration surfaces new open product decisions. Each entry records the question, the options the agent presented, the agent's recommendation with evidence, and (once the user answers) the resolution.

Under `.kiro/agent-state/spec-review-agent/<session-id>/`:
- `resume_state.md` — includes `consecutive_clean_AB` counter and the recent-C+D history for stuck-state detection.
- `iteration_log.md`
- `evidence_ledger.md`
- `mcp_transcripts.md`
- `web_research_log.md`
- `codebase_inspection_log.md`
- `pattern_mining_log.md` — records of pattern-mining findings across the codebase (per Q3.2 deep inspection).

Final chat message: the verdict (READY / READY-WITH-MINOR-DEFICITS / NOT-READY), the iteration number, the path to `review-latest.md`, and summary counts.

### Review-iteration file structure (fixed template)

Every `review-iteration-NN.md` file follows this template so the user can copy the full contents to Kiro IDE spec mode without further editing:

```
# Spec Review Iteration NN

**Spec directory:** .kiro/specs/<topic>/
**Reviewed files:** requirements.md, design.md, tasks.md  (whichever exist)
**Iteration:** NN
**Verdict:** READY | READY-WITH-MINOR-DEFICITS | NOT-READY
**consecutive_clean_AB:** <integer>

## Verdict Rationale
<why this verdict>

## A — Execution Blockers
<findings or "None">

## B — User-Intent Deviations
<findings or "None">

## C — Clarifications / Risks
<findings or "None">

## D — Minor Nits
<findings or "None">

## Open Product Decisions
<items requiring user input, with options and evidence, or "None">

## Evidence Summary
<counts and notable sources: MCP lookups, web sources, codebase references, pattern-mining hits>

## Handoff Instructions
<explicit instructions the user can hand to Kiro IDE spec mode>
```

The "Handoff Instructions" section makes the file self-contained for hand-off, so the user can point Kiro IDE at `review-latest.md` unconditionally.



## Cluster 5 — Agent-specific behavior (RESOLVED)

### Q5.1 — Review finding taxonomy

**Answer: A / B / C / D four-layer taxonomy, confirmed as definitive.**

- **A — Execution Blockers.** Issues that prevent the spec from being implemented as written (missing prerequisites, contradictory requirements, unrunnable task sequences, referenced symbols that do not exist).
- **B — User-Intent Deviations / Gaps.** The spec is implementable but deviates from stated user intent or contains gaps where intent is not covered. Also includes cross-task dependency gaps where one task's output is needed by another but is not wired in.
- **C — Clarifications / Risks.** Under-specified areas, ambiguities that could lead to divergent implementations, assumptions that require explicit validation, risks that warrant mitigation wording in the spec.
- **D — Minor Nits.** Stylistic issues, wording improvements, small inconsistencies, formatting, dev-bias in examples (hardcoded environments, etc.).

This taxonomy drives:
- The termination logic (`consecutive_clean_AB` counter from Cluster 2).
- The review-iteration file structure (section headings from Cluster 4).
- Finding ID prefixes: `A1`, `A2`, `B1`, `C1`, `D1`, etc.

### Q5.2 — Finding ID persistence across iterations

**Answer: (c) — Hybrid approach with unambiguous cross-iteration references.**

Rules:

1. **Fresh numbering per iteration is the primary convention.** Each review-iteration-NN.md numbers findings from 1 within its own severity sections (A1, A2, ..., B1, B2, ..., C1, ..., D1, ...).

2. **Recurrence annotations when the agent is confident.** When a current finding is recognizably the same issue as a previous iteration's finding (same file, same claim, same mismatch), the agent adds an annotation in the current finding, for example:

   ```
   ### A2 — Task 16 still references removed constant
   *Previously reported as A3 in review-iteration-02, A2 in review-iteration-03.*
   
   <finding body>
   ```

3. **Ambiguity prevention is mandatory.** The agent MUST NOT emit an ambiguous cross-reference. If it is not certain the current finding is the same as the prior one, it treats them as distinct and does not annotate. The guiding principle is: it must always be clear which specific finding is being discussed, across any review file.

4. **IDs are never reused within a single iteration.** Once retired (resolved in a prior iteration), an ID is not re-used for a new finding in the same severity section of a later iteration unless the annotation clearly identifies the new finding as distinct.

5. **The running `review-log.md` uses a stable identifier scheme.** For cross-iteration aggregation, each finding is identified by `iter-NN/A2` form (e.g., `iter-03/A2`). This gives a globally-unique handle independent of any recurrence logic.

### Q5.3 — Granularity of `prompt-discussion.md`

**Answer: (b) — Structured Q&A, organized by topic and decision.**

`prompt-discussion.md` structure:
- Organized by topic/decision clusters (similar to how the clusters in the current discussion file are organized).
- Each entry records:
  - The decision or question at stake.
  - The agent's synthesized question with the reasoning behind it.
  - The evidence the agent gathered to inform the question (MCP citations, web sources, codebase references).
  - The user's answer.
  - The resolution recorded as a concrete statement ("The prompt will specify X because Y").
- No verbatim transcript. Raw back-and-forth messages are not retained; the synthesized record is the authoritative artifact.
- Written at the end of Phase A as a single coherent document, not appended incrementally during the interview. (The agent holds the conversation in its session state during the interview and emits the structured discussion file once the `prompt.md` content is agreed.)

Rationale: verbatim transcripts in the old `prompts/*Discussion.txt` files were difficult to navigate. A structured, synthesized record provides the same audit value with better readability, and aligns with the user's goal of retiring the `prompts/` directory in favor of clean artifacts under `.kiro/specs/<topic>/`.

---

# Resolution Summary — All Open Items Resolved

All five clusters (12 questions plus follow-ups) from the end of the discussion above have been resolved. The inputs are now sufficient to draft the two agent prompts.

**Agent architecture (final):**
- **`spec-prompt-author-agent`** (Phase A) — interactive prompt authoring from a blank or seed idea to `prompt.md` + `prompt-discussion.md`.
- **`spec-review-agent`** (Phase B) — autonomous per-invocation review of Kiro-IDE-generated specs, emitting `review-iteration-NN.md` + `review-latest.md` + `review-log.md` with A/B/C/D findings and a READY / READY-WITH-MINOR-DEFICITS / NOT-READY verdict.

**Key design decisions:**
- Hybrid model — agents review only; Kiro IDE spec mode applies changes (Q1.1).
- Two separate agents rather than one two-mode agent (Q1.2a).
- All artifacts under `.kiro/specs/<topic>/`; `prompts/` directory retired (Q1.2b).
- Convergence termination: at least 5 consecutive clean-of-A/B iterations plus C/D stability for READY (Q2.1).
- Selective user input via structured review-file sections, mandatory self-resolution first, persisted resolutions (Q2.2).
- All three evidence sources (MCP, web, codebase) in scope for both agents (Q3.1).
- Deep codebase inspection with pattern mining and steering-document authority (Q3.2).
- No test execution; spec-readiness review only (Q3.3).
- Explicit directory-path input; Phase A asks topic as first question; Phase B asks for disambiguation if ambiguous (Q4.1).
- `review-latest.md` as stable Kiro-IDE handoff pointer; fixed review-iteration template with Handoff Instructions section (Q4.2).
- A/B/C/D taxonomy definitive (Q5.1).
- Hybrid finding-ID persistence with recurrence annotations and globally-unique `iter-NN/severity-N` handles (Q5.2).
- Structured (non-verbatim) `prompt-discussion.md` (Q5.3).

The next step is to draft the two agent prompts in the house style of the existing `doc-reviewer-agent` and `dead-code-removal-agent`.
